title: Meeting 7: Point estimation
text:
During the seminar
A field experiment motivates the difference-in-means estimator. We distinguish an estimand, an estimator, and an estimate, then examine unbiasedness, sampling variability, mean squared error, and consistency.
Potential outcomes help separate random assignment from random sampling and explain why a comparison under self-selection can miss the average treatment effect. Demos 1-4 prepare for B3, including exact enumeration of assignments, repeated studies, and summaries and CDFs of their estimates.
The final slide sequence and Demos 5-7 are optional. They revisit estimated standard errors, the exact t distribution under Normal observations, and the large-sample Normal approximation.

title: Meeting 7: Point estimation

B3 is due October 21 at 1:30 p.m. Pacific. Accept your private repository invitation and follow its README. The hypothetical village data and helpers are included. Complete the QMD’s code and written responses, run the completion check, and render a fresh HTML. Commit and push both the QMD and current HTML.
Keep track of what changes in each simulation: treatment assignment, sampled villages, the number of villages per study, or the number of simulation repetitions. These produce different kinds of variation.

title: Meeting 5: Continuous random variables
text:
During the seminar
We will distinguish point probabilities, densities, and cumulative probabilities. Integrals describe accumulated area, with geometry and R doing the calculations. No hand evaluation of complicated integrals is needed.
We will examine normal CDFs, forecast probabilities, quantiles, and simulation. A discrete vote-count model illustrates the normal approximation and continuity correction. Bargaining and contract examples show how transformations change the distribution of payoffs, and why a mean alone does not describe a decision.

title: Meeting 3: Conditional probability and Bayes’ rule
text:
During the seminar
We will distinguish conditional from marginal probabilities, examine independence, and use the law of total probability. A hypothetical arrest tree will provide the derivation of Bayes’ rule before the break.
After the break, we will solve Monty Hall analytically and simulate the host’s actions. A model of competing coalitions will illustrate conditioning on a first step and simulating a complete process. In each example, identify the reference group used in the denominator of a conditional probability.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text: You do not need to master all of Git to succeed in this course. POLI 210 uses a simple workflow: each assignment begins in a private GitHub repository, you work on a local copy in RStudio, and you push a sequence of commits back to GitHub. This page is the course reference for that workflow.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
What the tools are







Term
Meaning in this course




Git
Software on your computer that records changes to files as a history of snapshots.


GitHub
A website that stores a remote copy of a Git repository and runs assignment checks.


Repository
A project folder together with its Git history. We often shorten this to repo.


RStudio Project
The local working folder you open through its .Rproj file. RStudio’s Git pane gives you buttons for common Git operations.


GitHub Actions
The automated checks that run on GitHub after you push.



Git and GitHub are related but not identical. Git works locally and can record commits without an internet connection. GitHub stores the remote repository; it only receives a local commit after you push it.
GitHub: private remote repository and Actions
                  ^ push
                  |                 clone once / pull updates
                  |                           |
Your computer: edit -> save -> stage -> commit






ImportantSave, commit, and push are different



Save updates a file on your computer. Commit records a selected set of saved changes in the local Git history. Push sends local commits to GitHub. A saved answer is not submitted until its commit has been pushed.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
Vocabulary for the homework workflow

Clone: Make the initial local copy of a GitHub repository, including its history and connection back to GitHub. Clone once per assignment.
Diff: A line-by-line view of what changed since the last commit. Green lines were added; red lines were removed.
Stage: Select the saved changes that belong in the next commit. In RStudio, check a file in the Git pane to stage it.
Commit: Record the staged changes as a local snapshot with a short message explaining the work.
Push: Send local commits to the GitHub repository.
Pull: Bring remote commits into the local repository. In an individual assignment this is usually needed only if the instructor has updated the repository or you edited it from another computer.
Working tree: Git’s name for the files currently in your local project folder.
main: The single branch used for POLI 210 assignments. You do not need to create other branches.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
The course workflow

Once for each assignment

Accept the private repository invitation from GitHub.
On GitHub, select Code, choose HTTPS, and copy the URL.
In RStudio, choose File -> New Project -> Version Control -> Git.
Paste the URL and clone into your local Documents/POLI210 folder.
Open the project through its .Rproj file.

See GitHub and RStudio workflow for the illustrated menu sequence and authentication advice. Do not download the assignment as a ZIP file; a ZIP does not include the Git history or the connection to GitHub.


During every work session

Open the correct .Rproj file and confirm the project name in RStudio.
Run git status in the Terminal. If the working tree is clean and you need an instructor update, run git pull --ff-only.
Edit and save a small, meaningful part of the assignment.
Render the Quarto document and run the assignment’s local check.
Inspect each changed file’s diff in the Git pane.
Stage the files that belong together.
Commit with a descriptive message such as Complete Part 2.
Push, then inspect the newest run under GitHub’s Actions tab.

Repeat the edit-to-push cycle several times. Small commits are easier to understand and recover than one enormous final commit.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
Commands you will actually use
Run these in RStudio’s Terminal, from the assignment’s project folder. They are Git commands, not R code, so do not enter them in the R Console. The commands are the same on macOS and Windows; only the terminal prompt and the way a full file path is written may look different.







Command
What it tells Git to do




git status
Summarize the current branch, saved changes, staged changes, and commits not yet pushed. This is the best first diagnostic command.


git diff
Show saved changes that have not been staged. RStudio’s Diff button shows the same basic information.


git diff --staged
Show exactly what the next commit will contain.


git add a1-reproducible-workflow.qmd
Stage one file. For later assignments, substitute the actual filename. Checking a file in RStudio’s Git pane does this too.


git commit -m "Complete Part 2"
Record the staged changes locally with a message. RStudio’s Commit window does the same thing.


git push
Send local commits to GitHub.


git pull --ff-only
Bring down remote commits, but stop instead of creating an unexpected merge commit.


git log --oneline -5
Show the five most recent local commits.


git remote -v
Show which GitHub repository the local project is connected to.



You may also see the command-line form git clone REPOSITORY-URL. In this course, use RStudio’s new-project menu to clone so that it creates and opens the RStudio Project correctly.






TipRead git status literally




Changes not staged for commit means Git sees saved changes that are not yet selected for a commit.
Changes to be committed means files are staged for the next commit.
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' means you have local commits to push.
nothing to commit, working tree clean means Git sees no uncommitted saved changes.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
Common problems

My change is not in the Git pane
Save the file, then run git status. Also confirm that you opened the correct .Rproj file and edited the copy inside that project. See the file-path guide if you may have two copies of the assignment.


GitHub does not show my latest work
A save or local commit does not update GitHub. Run git status, commit any intended changes, and push. On GitHub, confirm that the newest commit message matches the one you just made.


Push was rejected or mentions non-fast-forward
Do not force-push. First run git status. If the working tree is clean, run git pull --ff-only and read the result. If Git refuses or reports a conflict, stop and send the instructor the exact message before trying more commands.


I staged the wrong file
Uncheck it in RStudio’s Git pane, or run:
git restore --staged FILENAME
This removes the file from the staging area without deleting your saved edits.


The newest GitHub Action failed
Open the newest run, expand the failed step, and read the first useful error. Confirm that the run used your newest commit. An Action failure does not erase your work; it means the remote check found something to repair.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
Safety rules

Work in the RStudio Project copy, not in a downloaded ZIP or a second copy.
Do not edit the same assignment alternately in RStudio and GitHub’s web editor; that creates two changing copies that must be reconciled.
Do not run git init inside a cloned assignment.
Do not use git push --force, git reset --hard, or delete the hidden .git folder. Ask for help before using a command that discards or rewrites work.
Never commit passwords, access tokens, or other secrets.
Before following a Git command from a web search or AI tool, make sure you understand what it changes. When uncertain, show the proposed command and current git status to the instructor first.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
Before you finish an assignment

The Quarto document renders successfully.
The local assignment check completes as expected.
The diff contains your intended work and no secrets or accidental files.
Your commits have descriptive messages.
git status says the working tree is clean and the branch is up to date with origin/main.
GitHub shows your newest commit and its newest Action run.

title: Git and GitHub field guide
text:
Optional deeper references
The material above is sufficient for the normal POLI 210 workflow. If you want more detail:

GitHub’s About Git explains version control, repositories, and how GitHub relates to Git.
GitHub’s Getting changes from a remote repository explains clone, fetch, and pull.

title: POLI 210: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data I
POLI 210: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data I
text:
6.1 Type A assignments
Type A assignments develop a specific statistical or computing skill. They are shorter and more structured than Type B assignments and will make the greatest use of automated feedback. Some tests will be visible so that students can check and improve their work before the deadline. Written interpretation and code quality will still be reviewed by the instructor.
Unless an assignment says otherwise, Type A work is individual.

title: POLI 210: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data I
text:
6.2 Type B assignments
Type B assignments ask students to combine statistical tools with substantive reasoning, usually using political or social data. Automated checks will focus on whether the project renders and whether core computations are reproducible; interpretation, argument, and presentation will be graded by the instructor.
Students may discuss Type B assignments and work through problems in groups of two or three. Each student must write, code, and submit an individual solution in their own repository, identify collaborators, and be able to explain every part of the submission. Copying another person’s code or prose is not collaboration.

title: POLI 210: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data I
text:
6.3 Assignment deadlines and extensions
Assignments are due at 1:30 p.m. on the dates listed below. Because solutions and feedback may be discussed soon after a deadline, late submissions are not ordinarily accepted. If illness, disability, caregiving, religious observance, or another serious circumstance affects your work, contact the instructor as early as reasonably possible so that an appropriate plan can be made. University-approved accommodations apply.

title: POLI 210: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data I

6.4 Take-home final
The final is cumulative and will assess statistical reasoning, interpretation, and reproducible analysis. Students will receive a 24-hour window during the official December 12-18 final-examination period. The exact start and end times will be scheduled in consultation with the class near the end of the semester; permitted resources will be announced with the exam instructions.

title: File paths and project folders
text:
A file path tells the computer where a file or folder is located. An absolute path begins at the top of one computer’s file system:
Those paths work only on Avery’s computer. Course code should instead use a path relative to the project root - the folder containing the .Rproj file:
That path works on macOS, Windows, another student’s computer, and GitHub Actions.

title: File paths and project folders
text:
Symbols and separators

Use forward slashes / in R paths on both macOS and Windows.
A single period . means the current folder.
Two periods .. mean the parent folder.
Put a path containing spaces inside quotation marks.
Match capitalization exactly: Data/file.csv and data/file.csv may be different paths on GitHub’s Linux runner.

title: File paths and project folders
text:
Three diagnostic questions
Run these in the R Console:
getwd()                                  # Where is R starting?
list.files()                             # What is in that folder?
file.exists("data/district_turnout.csv") # Can R find this path?
If the answers are surprising, open the .Rproj file and repair the relative path. Do not solve a submitted path problem with setwd() or file.choose(); those depend on one computer or on interactive input.

title: File paths and project folders

In RStudio, choose File → New Project → Version Control → Git.
Paste the URL into Repository URL.
Choose your local Documents/POLI210 folder as the parent directory.

Cloning is a one-time operation. It creates the working files and a hidden .git directory containing the repository history. Downloading a ZIP file does not create that history and is not a substitute for cloning.

title: GitHub and RStudio workflow
text:
The cycle you repeat
edit → save → inspect diff → stage → commit → push → inspect Actions

Save writes the current file on your computer.
Diff shows exactly what changed.
Stage selects changes for the next snapshot.
Commit records that snapshot locally with a message.
Push sends local commits to GitHub.
Actions repeats the assignment’s checks on a clean remote computer.

Use short, descriptive commit messages such as Add my name, Complete vector exercises, or Render final report. Do not use one enormous final commit.

title: GitHub and RStudio workflow
text:
Local checks
Assignments may include a command such as:
Rscript checks/check-a1.R
Run it in RStudio’s Terminal, not the R Console. Read the first failed check, make one focused repair, and rerun it. After pushing, repeat that process with the newest run in GitHub’s Actions tab.

title: GitHub and RStudio workflow
text:
Authentication problems
GitHub account passwords cannot be used as Git passwords. If cloning or pushing opens a browser, sign into the correct GitHub account and authorize the request. If the repository cannot be found, first confirm that you accepted its invitation and that RStudio is using the expected account.
Never paste a password or token into a Quarto file, R script, commit, screenshot, or help request.

title: Install and verify the software

Git
Install Git from git-scm.com. In RStudio’s Terminal, run:
git --version
Then record the name that should appear on your commits:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "YOUR_GITHUB_EMAIL"
Use an email recognized by your GitHub account or the private noreply address shown in GitHub’s email settings. These commands configure authorship; they do not sign you into GitHub.

title: Meeting 2: Probability and simulation
section: By the end of the seminar
text:
By the end of the seminar
You should be able to define a sample space and event, distinguish equally likely from unequally likely outcomes, use complement and union rules, and calculate finite probabilities by counting when the assumptions permit it.
You should also be able to simulate a complete trial with sample(), repeat trials with replicate(), and estimate an event probability using a logical comparison and mean(). We will compare exact and simulated answers using dice, random treatment assignment, hypothetical polling, and committee selection.

title: Meeting 4: Discrete random variables
text:
During the seminar
We will map outcomes to numerical values, construct probability mass functions, and compare exact calculations with simulated experiments. A voter-mobilization example connects enumeration and counting to treatment counts.
We will use a polling model to study binomial counts and cumulative probabilities, then examine transformations, expectation, variance, and independence. A waiting-time example distinguishes failures before a first success from the total number of calls.

title: Meeting 4: Discrete random variables
text:
After class
Rerun the demonstrations and change one input at a time. Explain the difference between increasing the number of voters in a poll and increasing the number of simulated polls. Practice translating each probability inequality into an R expression.
Assignment instructions and submission repositories are distributed separately through the private-repository workflow.

title: Meeting 6: Sampling distributions
text:
During the seminar
We will connect histogram areas and kernel smoothing to last week’s concept of density. Repeated samples let us study a statistic as another random variable and distinguish sample size from simulation repetitions.
The LLN describes concentration of sample means, while the CLT describes their standardized limiting shape. We will compare simulated cumulative probabilities with a Normal approximation, including a repeat with a different seed. Squared deviations and estimated standard errors motivate the chi-squared and t distributions.
Demo 8b explains the functions, lists, and CDF comparison used in A4. Demo 11 computes the t statistic from each sample and compares two-sided tail probabilities. The F and unbiasedness previews are optional.

When exploring the demo, change n and B separately. Explain which change alters the sampling distribution and which changes the simulation’s precision. Use the probability comparisons alongside the plots, not as a claim that every aspect of the distribution is Normal.

title: Meeting 8: Data wrangling with dplyr
text:
During the seminar
Congressional elections and ultimatum-game data provide examples of selecting columns, filtering and sorting rows, creating variables with mutate(), and summarizing groups. We distinguish missing values from zeros and explore lower and upper bounds for missing minimum acceptable offers.
We then practice working with text, reshaping tables, combining rows, and joining datasets. Join audits check whether keys are unique, whether rows were unexpectedly duplicated, and whether any records failed to match. The demo includes frozen teaching datasets and source documentation, so no in-class data downloads are required.

Keep track of what each row represents before and after a transformation. In particular, counting rows is not always the same as summing the counts stored in a column.
